chunks: Al-Husayn b. Ahmad narrated to us. He said: My father narrated to us. He said: Muhammad b. Abi al-Sahban narrated to us. He said: Abu Ahmad Muhammad b. Ziyad al-Azdi narrated to us. He said: Aban al-Ahmar narrated to me from al-Sadiq Ja'far b. Muhammad, peace be upon him.

A man came to him and said: May my mother and father be sacrificed for you, O son of the Messenger of Allah! Teach me a proverb. So he said: If Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, has guaranteed sustenance, then why are you worried? If sustenance is allotted, then why be greedy? If the Judgment is true, then why go to gatherings? If the reward is from Allah, then why be lazy? If the future is truly from Allah, then why be miserly? If the punishment from Allah is the Fire, then why sin? If death is true, then why be gleeful? If the offer of Allah is true, then why plot? If Satan is the enemy, then why be heedless? If passing through the Path is true, then why be astonished? If all things are destined, then why be sorrowful? If this world is fleeting, then why be content with it?

key_terms.الصراط: al-Sirat - the Path over Hellfire on Judgment Day

ai.seo_question: What are Imam al-Sadiq's twelve rhetorical questions about faith and trust in God?
ai.summary: A man approaches Imam al-Sadiq asking for an admonition. The Imam responds with twelve powerful rhetorical questions, each following the pattern 'If X is true, then why Y?' The questions address: (1) worry despite God's guarantee of sustenance, (2) greed despite allotted provisions, (3) hoarding despite the certainty of Judgment, (4) laziness despite God's reward, (5) miserliness despite God's promise of replacement, (6) sinning despite God's punishment being the Fire, (7) joy despite the certainty of death, (8) plotting despite accountability before God, (9) heedlessness despite Satan being the enemy, (10) self-admiration despite crossing the Path, (11) sorrow despite all being by divine decree, and (12) contentment with this world despite its transience. This teaching was delivered during the Amali lecture gatherings of 367 AH.
